item.title: MAGA’s Talarico conspiracy theory has no “off” switch
item.description: The American right’s epistemic closure is a thing to behold
item.content:encoded:
By Jeremiah Johnson

Reminder: Join The Argument this week for a live event on Oct. 16 in Washington, D.C.!

Liberalism isn’t just about designing optimal technocratic policies — it’s about building a society where people have the freedom to create great art. Great art doesn’t have to be irreproachable to be worth reading; you don’t have to agree with Plato to learn from him.

Few people make that case better than Naomi Kanakia, who writes the popular literary newsletter Woman of Letters. Jerusalem Demsas will be interviewing her about her new book, What’s So Great About the Great Books?

The conversation kicks off at 7 p.m. at Solid State Books (600F H St. NE). [Details here].

In 2010, the libertarian writer Julian Sanchez accused the American conservative movement of “epistemic closure.” The right had spent decades building an alternative media ecosystem, and Sanchez was concerned about the health of that ecosystem.

Conservative media, he argued, had become increasingly self-contained and insular. It boxed out all but its own sources and its own interpretations of events, thanks to a reflexive hostility toward information originating outside the conservative bubble. Sanchez’s insight was that conservatives weren’t too closed-minded — if anything, their insular media world made them too open to nearly any bizarre or outlandish story, provided that story came from trusted voices within their own ranks.

Sanchez wrote about that problem over 16 years ago. In 2026, things have gotten considerably worse. The frightening thing now is that declining standards at conservative media institutions are the least of our worries — because those institutions are being eclipsed by more powerful voices online and in the White House.

Share

Between the unchecked agenda-setting power of right-wing influencers and a Trump-controlled Republican Party fully committed to instrumental lies and misinformation, any truth-seeking actors within conservative media now seem to be fully obsolete. They turned on the conspiracy machine for cynical political reasons, but they’re increasingly realizing that the machine doesn’t have an off switch.

Conspiracies all the way down

These dynamics were perfectly demonstrated by the fracas that followed Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico’s disappearance from the campaign trail earlier this month. Talarico spent the first week of October off the campaign trail, at home in Texas recovering from the flu. There was never any mystery about what was happening: He appeared virtually at an event where he told attendees that he had come down with the flu.

But that didn’t stop Talarico’s opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, from demanding “proof of life,” setting up a tip line for information about Talarico’s location, and leading a “Where is James Talarico?” chant at a rally. Trump declared the Democrat “MISSING IN ACTION” in a Truth Social rant. (He also called him “James TalaFREAKo.”)

Talarico appeared at a music festival in Austin on Oct. 9, and he attended a Kacey Musgraves concert in Dallas the following day. But during his absence, right-wing influencers began promoting a theory that Talarico wasn’t sick at all. Instead, they claimed he had suffered a nervous breakdown and had been secretly admitted to a psychiatric hospital.

The theory went viral just as Talarico was emerging from his illness, thanks to repeated posts from personalities such as Jan. 6 organizer Caroline Wren and former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt. (Pratt even claimed to have “sources” confirming the story.)

On Sunday, MAGA influencers Nick Sortor and Rhein Amacher claimed they had real proof: An employee at a psychiatric hospital in Ohio had allegedly admitted, in a phone call to Amacher, that Talarico was a patient. Right-wing social media absolutely erupted in anticipation of a scandal that would destroy Talarico’s credibility and thus his campaign.

Nobody in the MAGA media sphere seemed to notice the story’s obvious problems. For one, Sortor and Amacher’s “proof” supposedly described Talarico checking out of the Ohio facility on Saturday. But Talarico, as noted above, was demonstrably present at the Austin City Limits Music Festival on Friday. And in the full audio of Amacher’s phone call, which was obtained by The Bulwark, the Ohio hospital employee repeatedly denies that there’s anyone named James Talarico in the hospital’s system.

Later Sunday evening, the hospital itself flatly denied that Talarico had ever been a patient, killing the conspiracy for good.

Haha, just kidding! Despite the overwhelming evidence against the “Talarico was institutionalized” story, it kept circulating. And it wasn’t just anonymous accounts: Former Fox News personality Megyn Kelly was still demanding answers after the hospital’s denial, and White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller kept conspiracy-posting even after The New York Times confirmed with time-stamped security images that Talarico was at his home just as he claimed.

Subscribe now

To some on the right, the very fact that they got embarrassed was its own form of conspiracy. Once it became clear that there was no evidence for the mental breakdown thesis, conservatives began to blame Talarico for not heading off the false story effectively enough.

Trump-friendly blogger Mickey Kaus wondered why Talarico never announced his illness with a tweet. Washington Free Beacon reporter Chuck Ross seemed unable to believe that the campaign wouldn’t release photos of a bedridden Talarico to clear his name. The Current Revolt podcast asked why the Talarico campaign hadn’t said anything (it had). Perhaps it was a false flag, suggested @CynicalPublius, one of the influencers who were secretly installed as a Department of Defense employee under Secretary Pete Hegseth.

What we’re witnessing here is a group of people grasping for a meta-conspiracy theory in order to avoid the dawning realization that they were set up — by their own side.

Are there any gates left to keep?

The epistemic closure that Sanchez described in 2010 is now overwhelming in right-wing circles. It has made conservative media incredibly vulnerable to failure modes such as the one we saw in the Talarico conspiracy theorizing. And social media compounds the problem further by destroying the ability of traditional media gatekeepers to keep out bad information.

One of the most interesting details to emerge from this entire episode is what happened before Nick Sortor posted his supposed scoop. According to reporting from Current Revolt, Amacher, who made the phone call to the Ohio psychiatric hospital where Talarico was falsely reported to be hospitalized, said that he initially pitched the story to The Blaze and the Daily Mail. But the story didn’t pass legal muster with those outlets, despite their ideological sympathy.

Instead, Amacher turned to Sortor, who is essentially a random grifter and was happy to blast the allegation out to millions of people on social media.

Before the rise of social media, getting repeatedly turned down by formal publications would have been the end of the road for a story like this. But today, algorithmic incentives dominate professional standards. Amacher himself acknowledged that influencers aren’t held to the same standards as journalists.

Whatever vestigial safeguards still exist at institutions like the Daily Mail or Fox News are so easily bypassed on social media that they’ve been rendered obsolete. Gatekeepers used to have enormous power to determine what stories became news and which withered on the vine, but social media has eroded that power.

In practice, gatekeeping is dying. Con artists can go viral and drive national stories without institutional help.

This all starts, of course, at the top. Technology alone can’t explain how we got here, or why the problem is so acute in conservative circles. President Donald Trump, for essentially as long as he has been in public life, has been a connoisseur of conspiracy theories. He lies as easily as he breathes, so much so that one can’t help but wonder whether he even understands the concept of truth at all. Maybe expecting him to be honest is like lecturing a raccoon about property rights as it rummages through your trash.

In 2008, the late Sen. John McCain famously shut down a woman spreading conspiratorial views about then-Sen. Barack Obama at one of McCain’s campaign rallies. In those days, Fox News was certainly biased, but it still maintained a certain level of professionalism and would have been loath to broadcast completely unsubstantiated claims.

But Trump was the exact opposite of McCain. Just a few years after McCain’s act of decency, Trump was eagerly spreading lies that Obama had not been born in the U.S. and demanding to see a birth certificate. And under Trump’s malign influence, the entire conservative media ecosystem has corrupted itself.

Subscribe now

Conservative media now selects for loyalty and against competency and honesty. That’s why Fox News had to pay $787.5 million to Dominion Voting Systems in a defamation suit concerning Trump’s claims that the 2020 election was stolen. And Fox, despite its decline, is sadly still among the more responsible actors in this space.

MAGA has plenty of people calling themselves “investigative journalists” these days, but almost none of them are competent and honest. Christopher Rufo remains a conservative power broker despite spreading lies about Haitian immigrants eating cats in 2024. Dinesh D’Souza’s documentary 2,000 Mules, which purported to prove that the 2020 election was stolen, was so dishonest that its distributor eventually apologized and withdrew it. James O’Keefe has built a career on amateurish sting operations and selectively edited recordings. Yet figures like these continue to command attention in conservative media.

The rot runs deep, and it runs through the entire MAGA movement. Many of those who spread the most baseless rumors on social media also work for the administration.

To a first approximation, there are no responsible MAGA journalists. There is no last redoubt, no “good ones” who are pro-Trump but still cling to honesty and competency. Anyone who could have been that type of bulwark left for, well, The Bulwark. The mainstream of conservative American media is now just baseless, vile conspiracism. And the bad news is that there is no bottom.

It can always get worse, and it probably will. After all, the White House just chose a new press secretary who is a Pizzagate conspiracist and has reposted claims about how Michelle Obama has a penis.

This isn’t a both-sides issue. The left wing of American politics has a number of its own problems, and plenty of liberal voices have embarrassed themselves by spreading misinformation. But there’s substantial evidence that conservative social media users share more low-quality information than liberal users do.

A 2023 study in Science found that conservatives were in a deeper social media bubble than liberals and that misinformation was more concentrated inside that conservative bubble, with “no equivalent on the liberal side.”

The Talarico conspiracy is disturbing, but it’s not unique. This kind of wild misinformation is becoming more and more frequent in conservative circles. The upshot here is that conservatives in America are losing the ability to self-correct — and are thereby frequently losing touch with reality. This is happening at the very bottom, with anonymous social media profiles, and it extends all the way to the top and the man in the Oval Office.

Any movement that prizes loyalty above truth will eventually lose its ability to distinguish reality from fiction. And once it loses that ability, there’s no obvious mechanism to bring it back.

item.title: The book is not about you
item.description: Some readers want every protagonist to be a version of themselves. They’re missing one of fiction’s greatest pleasures.
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

On today’s episode of The Argument podcast, Matt Yglesias and I cancel and uncancel some historical figures. Paid subscribers can watch or listen to the episode ad free here or read the transcript at the end of this post. Free subscribers can watch the episode on YouTube here or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Like many girls of my generation, I read Twilight in middle school. One thing that was notable about the book was author Stephenie Meyer’s reticence to provide her main character, Bella Swan, with many distinguishing physical descriptors. In the novel, she is generically described as “slender, but soft somehow” as well as pale with brown hair. This wasn’t just poor writing, it was, the author claims, a deliberate choice.

At the time, Meyer published an FAQ about the book on her website. One question asked, “What does Bella look like?” Here’s her answer:

“I left out a detailed description of Bella in the book so that the reader could more easily step into her shoes…Bella’s looks are open to interpretation.”

Meyer then gives a “detailed” description of what Bella looks like to her:

“In my head, Bella is very fair-skinned, with long, straight, dark brown hair and chocolate brown eyes. Her face is heart-shaped —a wide forehead with a widow’s peak, large, wide-spaced eyes, prominent cheekbones, and then a thin nose and a narrow jaw with a pointed chin. Her lips are a little out of proportion, a bit too full for her jaw line. Her eyebrows are darker than her hair and more straight than they are arched. She’s five foot four inches tall, slender but not at all muscular, and weighs about 115 pounds. She has stubby fingernails because she has a nervous habit of biting them.”

Robert Pattinson, who would go on to play Edward Cullen, Bella’s love interest, in the Twilight movie, said in a 2008 interview that “When I read it I was convinced Stephenie was convinced she was Bella.”

Meyer herself appeared in the film adaptations of two of her books: as a cafe customer in Twilight and a wedding guest in Breaking Dawn Part 1. A cameo offers another way into fiction: Perhaps you can’t become the heroine but you can at least be a part of her world.

What looks like an inconsequential episode of authorial self-insertion belongs to a long tradition of treating fiction as a vehicle for wish fulfillment. We can become someone more desired or extraordinary, or simply find a place in a world more exciting than our own. But when finding that place becomes a requirement of enjoying a book, a protagonist’s difference starts to look like a defect in the story. Her tastes, desires, and choices become obstacles to our participation and we lose one of fiction’s greatest pleasures: becoming absorbed in someone else’s life without needing that life to accommodate our own.

Subscribe now

Main character energy

I flashed back to my Twilight years after watching Twitter debate a book content creator’s viral provocation about whether readers self-insert as the protagonist or a side character:

Both answers assumed I needed a part in the story, but I thought being the reader was enough. I could care desperately about what happened to a character, sympathize with her struggles or be furious at her choices, without ever imagining myself a part of any of it. (It’s also not the first time this type of discourse has taken off.)

Some of this seems to be downstream of the growing influence of fanfiction over traditional publishing. For decades now, “reader-inserts” have proliferated on public writing sites like Archive of Our Own.

The term “reader-insert” refers to a genre of fanfiction that places the reader in the story, often using “Y/N” as a stand-in for your name rather than a protagonist’s name. These stories are typically written in second person, and sometimes writers will even leave room for readers to put in their own hair color, eye color, or other distinguishing characteristic.

Y/N is the extreme case, but you don’t need a blank for your name to read this way. Many readers demand first-person perspectives in order to insert themselves more easily into the story. For a reader who has confused herself with the heroine, third person is a constant reminder that someone else actually is — and it turns out a lot of readers experience that distance as a flaw.

In March of this year, Luke Winkie wrote a piece in Slate about romance fiction readers who refuse to read books in third person. As Winkie documents, readers’ stated reasons for preferring a first-person point of view include a desire for escapism and identification and also the baffling revelation that some readers find third person harder to read: “readers mourn their own self-diagnosed ineptitude; they’d like to savor the richness of third person, they say, but, for whatever reason, are unable to wrap their minds around the vantage point.”

One romance author tells Winkie that she has had readers come up to her at book signings “and say, to my face, ‘I won’t read this book of yours because it’s in third person.’”

Some readers have the opposite opinion and hate first-person because they find the narrator’s behavior or thinking different from their own:

In her 2014 New Yorker article “The Scourge of Relatability,” Rebecca Mead derides those who demand art act as “a selfie: a flattering confirmation of an individual’s solipsism.” She goes on to argue that readers who demand this are lazy consumers of art: “to reject any work because we feel that it does not reflect us in a shape that we can easily recognize—because it does not exempt us from the active exercise of imagination or the effortful summoning of empathy—is our own failure.”

When novelist Claire Messud was interviewed about her then-latest book by Publishers Weekly, the interviewer said of her main character: “I wouldn’t want to be friends with Nora, would you?” Messud responded with disgust:

“For heaven’s sake, what kind of question is that? Would you want to be friends with Humbert Humbert? Would you want to be friends with Mickey Sabbath? Saleem Sinai? Hamlet? Krapp? Oedipus? Oscar Wao? Antigone? Raskolnikov? Any of the characters in The Corrections? Any of the characters in Infinite Jest? Any of the characters in anything Pynchon has ever written? Or Martin Amis? Or Orhan Pamuk? Or Alice Munro, for that matter? If you’re reading to find friends, you’re in deep trouble. We read to find life, in all its possibilities. The relevant question isn’t “is this a potential friend for me?” but “is this character alive?”

Subscribe now

That readers have strong preferences is nothing new. Some readers are precious about whether they will read hardcovers or paperbacks, others refuse to read genres like magical realism or think that dialogue without quotation marks is an unforgivable affectation. But those are preferences about the book, whereas a demand for perfect identification with the main character is something else — it’s a demand that the author have nothing to say or communicate that is outside of a reader’s own experience.

The appeal of reader-inserts is comprehensible. A story can give us the pleasure of being desired, admired, or unusually important or talented. If I can take the place of a brilliant artist or ingenious politician, it allows me to pretend I have those traits as well. But what room does that leave for someone whose desires we don’t share? Whose decisions frustrate, stun, or disgust us? How about a reader whose life we would never want?

What I’m worried about is twofold: First, that people will fail to develop the capacity to find value in the experience of another person without needing it to feel indistinguishable from their own; second, that authors are willing to degrade their own art to meet this longstanding reader preference.

You are living in a fantasy (pejorative)

The desire to become the heroine predates the internet. So does the fear that readers might lose something by doing so.

In 1773, John Trumbull, a lawyer and satirical poet, mocked readers who imagined themselves as romantic heroines in his satirical narrative poem The Progress of Dulness: “For while she reads romance, the Fair one Fails not to think herself the Heroine…Thus Harriet reads, and reading really Believes herself a young Pamela.”

Trumbull’s aim was to show that women’s deficiencies arose from a lack of education; his worry was that this sort of self-identification would lead to an excess of self-flattery and that women would expect life to follow the script of unrealistic romances.

The concern that self-identification can cash out into false expectations is dramatized in Gustave Flaubert’s Madame Bovary: Emma Bovary interprets her own life through the romantic heroines of the novels she reads. After Emma begins her affair with Rodolphe, Flaubert writes that “She became herself, as it were, an actual part of these imaginings.”

Discerning readers will note the strain of paternalistic condescension toward female readers that is laced through much of this criticism, from Trumbull to the present. But charging critics with condescension doesn’t change the fact that this habit harms readers themselves.

These examples describe fears that readers will treat fiction-reading as wish-fulfillment. But a reader can understand perfectly well that a romance is a fantasy and still approach every character as a potential substitute for herself. The bigger question is if we can expect novels to teach us about something other than ourselves.

Vladimir Nabokov’s lecture that opened his Cornell literature course, “Good Readers and Good Writers,” engages directly with this question. In it, he recalls a short quiz he gave students at a “remote provincial college” about which of the following definitions made a good reader:

  1. The reader should belong to a book club.

  2. The reader should identify himself or herself with the hero or heroine.

  3. The reader should concentrate on the social-economic angle.

  4. The reader should prefer a story with action and dialogue to one with none.

  5. The reader should have seen the book in a movie.

  6. The reader should be a budding author.

  7. The reader should have imagination.

  8. The reader should have memory.

  9. The reader should have a dictionary.

  10. The reader should have some artistic sense.

This is what passed for survey evidence in Nabokov’s day unfortunately. He reports that “the students leaned heavily on emotional identification, action, and the social-economic or historical angle.”

For his part, Nabokov thought that “the worst thing a reader can do” is “identif[y] himself with a character in the book. This lowly variety is not the kind of imagination I would like readers to use.” Instead, he exhorts us to “remain a little aloof and take pleasure in this aloofness while at the same time we keenly enjoy—passionately enjoy, enjoy with tears and shivers—the inner weave of a given masterpiece.”

Take Nabokov’s most celebrated novel, Lolita, which is a first-person account of a very charismatic pedophile. Humbert Humbert is a cultivated, self-justifying creep who worms his way into the life of a 12-year-old American girl so he can abuse her, but the process of the reader discovering his true character and the unreliability of his own perspective is the point. Lolita lets us into Humbert Humbert’s head but the experience of horror as you recognize his evasions, resist his justifications, and wrench yourself away from appreciating the prose to confront the horror of his actions is what makes the first-person perspective valuable.

The tension is what makes his perspective so powerful: we are immersed in his account while struggling to preserve our own judgement. The “I” on the page belongs to Humbert. Nabokov leaves no room for wish fulfillment, and no one could wish to see themselves reflected in this narrator; the novel’s brilliance is its ability to put us into intimate contact with someone we have absolutely no wish to become.

What is the point of reading fiction?

The incentives here are quite bad for fiction. Meyer’s goal of making it easy for readers to pretend themselves to be Bella resulted in erasing the characteristics that made her a particular person. The risk is that the details that make a character distinct, that is human, come to seem like obstacles to the reader’s enjoyment. Elsewhere in her FAQ, Meyer explains that Bella is listening to Linkin Park in chapter seven, but that she omitted the band’s name because she worried it might no longer be cool by publication. But why would we want Bella’s taste to conform to the reader’s own? (Recently, readers noticed that the Kindle edition of Pretty Little Liars was quietly changed to modernize references from 2006 — a Fear Factor reference became a TikTok challenge, references to Snapchat, Instagram, Adele, and Billie Eilish also cropped up).

If every potential source of distance becomes a reason to withhold a detail, we lose opportunities to encounter someone whose tastes and attachments are her own. Which is, I contend, one of the best things about fiction.

In one of my favorite books, Never Let Me Go by Kazuo Ishiguro, I remember being furious with the narrator, Kathy. (Editor’s note: Spoiler incoming) Raised to surrender her organs until the donations kill her, she never fights back or stages the rebellion I kept wanting from her. Why didn’t she fight? Why didn’t she refuse? She was dying anyway. I was certain I would have.

The distance between me and Kathy forced me to ask harder questions about what caused those distinctions. Was it really just that I was more courageous than her or was it that I had not been raised to accept my own eventual dismemberment? How much of what I understood as free will depended on possibilities I had been taught to imagine?

Making Kathy behave as I wanted might have given me a more satisfying rebellion but it would have prevented me from engaging with the questions the author was raising.

The most self-flattering explanation for my disinclination for inserting myself wholly into the novels I read is that I had sophisticated literary instincts even as a child. I doubt it. I read plenty of books for the ordinary pleasures of suspense, romance, and escape.

More likely, there was just no way I was going to confuse myself with the narrators or the characters of the books I was reading. I wasn’t ivory-skinned like Bella, heir to a planetary dynasty like Paul Atreides, or an Englishwoman whose financial future depended on marrying well, like Elizabeth Bennet. And I certainly wasn’t being raised to surrender my organs like Kathy. These characters’ circumstances bore little resemblance to mine, and nevertheless I found myself absorbed in their hopes, furious at their choices, and devastated by their defeats. I didn’t need to be a part of their world to make them a part of mine.

item.title: Sorry lawyers, you can't save the planet with paperwork
item.description: Permitting reform won’t weaken environmental protections
item.content:encoded:
By Milan Singh

Welcome to The Closing Argument, our verdict on the news, plus everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict, by Milan Singh

Growing up, I was captivated by the BBC documentary series The Life of Birds, particularly Sir David Attenborough’s direct-to-camera address in the final episode.

“Now, we have taken over the Earth, the sea and the sky,” he says. “But with skill and care and knowledge, we can ensure that there is still a place on Earth for birds, in all their beauty and variety. If we want to — and surely, we should.”

I agree with him, and it’s why I’m sympathetic to the goals of the environmental movement. We should have strong environmental regulations to prevent wanton habitat destruction, even if those regulations involve some degree of economic inefficiency.

So I understand environmentalists’ hesitancy to support federal permitting reform efforts, such as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which is currently under consideration in Congress.

We know some degree of permitting reform is necessary for the fight against climate change — because we need to make it easier to build out solar, wind, batteries, and transmission lines that can carry clean energy — but it stands to reason that making it easier to build infrastructure might also make it easier to despoil natural environments.

Indeed, BAAJA includes reforms to a slew of environmental laws: the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act.

For this reason, some groups such as the Center for Biological Diversity have already announced opposition to the bill. But many of America’s most storied environmental organizations are still on the sidelines. The Sierra Club released a statement expressing concern about potential benefits for oil and gas companies, though it also said that it was “still reviewing this new 400+ page package.” The Natural Resources Defense Council’s statement said that there are “stark tradeoffs” in BAAJA but noted that “[i]t will take us time to digest this bill.”

What the green groups say could determine the fate of the bill. Many House Democrats who are on the fence are likely waiting to see how these groups weigh in, because their constituents take these organizations’ endorsements very seriously.

Luckily, after reading all 417 pages of the legislative text, I can confirm that BAAJA does not actually weaken the substantive protections that America’s environmental laws are meant to guarantee.

“I think when folks hear changes to the Clean Water Act or to the Endangered Species Act, you know, they’re thinking all of a sudden this is going to allow polluters to dump stuff into streams and lakes, or it’s going to allow folks to go out and take an endangered bird habitat and bulldoze. None of that is in this law,” Rep. Josh Harder, D-Calif. and chair of the bipartisan Build America caucus, told me.

What BAAJA will do is reform the procedural elements of the environmental laws that currently make it difficult to build new energy infrastructure — even if it can be demonstrated that this infrastructure does not involve illegal environmental harms.

In other words, BAAJA mostly just prevents environmental laws from being used for reasons other than their intended purposes. When you add in the bill’s likely benefits for climate, the result is a win for the environment overall.

Share

Procedure vs. substance

Most major environmental laws have two elements: procedural and substantive. Substantive elements are things such as the Endangered Species Act’s prohibition on killing, harming, or harassing an animal on the endangered species list. Procedural elements are things like mandating studies or reviews or other bureaucratic steps that, in and of themselves, do not directly protect the environment.

I could identify just one substantive change that the permitting reform bill would make to any of the environmental laws it targets.

Under Section 401 of the Clean Water Act, states (as well as federally recognized Native American tribes) can effectively veto federal permits for projects that would discharge into their waters. This makes sense! People don’t want pollution dumped into their water.

Section 1202 of BAAJA aims to fix a loophole some states have used to block fossil fuel infrastructure on pretextual grounds, at times by arguing that fossil fuel use causes climate change, and climate change could be bad for water quality. If BAAJA becomes law, certification denial will be allowed only if a state can provide clear and convincing evidence of specific water quality harms — and that no reasonable modifications would mitigate those harms. One of the bill’s authors, Senator Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., says that this change will also stop pretextual roadblocks for transmission lines as well.

In other words, if you want to stop a project based on a risk it will pollute the water, there actually has to be a risk it will pollute the water.

When it comes to the Endangered Species Act, BAAJA makes just one significant procedural change, imposing a 150-day statute of limitations for plaintiffs to seek an injunction or voiding of (part of) a permit if the underlying project threatens an endangered or threatened species. But it does not limit the ability of anyone to file legitimate suits within that window.

There is even less substance to the changes to the other laws. That’s because NEPA and NHPA are laws that only have procedural elements.

Here’s how NEPA works: Federal agencies have to produce detailed statements of the environmental impacts of “major federal actions.” If someone believes that the agency did not properly evaluate the environmental impact of a proposed action — such as the issuance of a permit for an energy project — then they can sue. If the court rules in the plaintiff’s favor, then the permit is vacated and sent back to the agency to start from scratch.

This process is easily abused. Even if a plaintiff knows their case is unlikely to hold up in court, they might litigate anyway. Maybe the goal is to delay the project while the agency redoes the permit, or to raise costs for the developer so much that the project no longer pencils out.

A report from the Breakthrough Institute analyzed 387 NEPA cases brought before appellate courts from 2013 to 2022. Federal agencies won 80% of the challenges — but those cases took more than four years to wrap up, adding substantial costs to the projects even though they were aboveboard.

Subscribe now

NHPA, which requires that federal agencies perform a review for projects that will affect historic sites, has been a tool for similar abuses: Plaintiffs can allege spurious harms, and lawsuits dragging on and on can significantly raise project costs.

BAAJA makes several changes to both laws. It imposes a series of deadlines for agencies to complete the review process. Any lawsuits based on NEPA or NHPA must be filed within 150 days of permits being issued, and lawsuits can only be filed by parties that participated in the public comment period during the permitting process and can demonstrate a direct harm.

Cases go straight to federal appellate courts — that way plaintiffs can’t cherry-pick district court judges who are ideologically aligned with them — and the courts are instructed to give “substantial deference” to the agencies’ decision-making. Most importantly, if a permit is found to be deficient in a particular area, then that part — and only that part — of the permit is returned to the agency to fix in 180 days or less.

This means that a successful lawsuit doesn’t kill an otherwise-good project that would’ve imposed a specific, fixable harm.

Presidents shouldn’t play politics with the environment

It is true that some elements of the bill would benefit oil and gas projects. But in the long run, making it easier to build energy infrastructure of all kinds will likely disproportionately benefit renewables, which are already beginning to crowd out fossil fuels’ role in meeting new demand in global energy markets.

To the extent that environmentalists don’t trust the Trump administration to play fair when it comes to renewable energy, they should support this bill.

President Donald Trump seems to have some sort of personal vendetta against wind projects and, to a lesser extent, solar power. His Interior Department issued stop-work orders to halt construction of five major offshore wind projects that had already been permitted, which has rightly irked environmentalists. Conservatives retort that this turnabout is fair play, given that the Biden administration yanked a permit for the Keystone XL pipeline.

One of BAAJA’s goals is to fix this tit-for-tat problem by tying the hands of presidents from either party, so they can’t abuse the permitting process to slow down energy projects they couldn’t block on the merits. Trump’s ability to meddle with already-permitted offshore wind projects will be limited. Future Democratic presidents won’t be able to pull permits for oil and gas projects that they don’t like.

For environmentalists, this bill is essentially a bet that, given an even playing field, renewables can outcompete fossil fuels. That’s a bet I think is worth taking.

Midterm update

Lakshya Jain, our director of political data, uses data from The Argument’s polling operation to inform the Split Ticket 2026 House and Senate models. Here’s his update on the state of play this week:

Democrats retain very strong odds to win the House of Representatives (89%) and their odds of taking the Senate have stabilized at 65%. While that’s roughly where things stood last week, there’s a new state in the “toss-up” column of our Senate forecast: Kansas, where we haven’t seen Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton trail in a poll for over a month. Between that and Josh Turek continuing to hang on at 50/50 odds in Iowa, Democrats have a lot of reason to feel optimistic — though they only need to look back to 2020 for a sobering reminder of what can happen if the polls are wrong.

These models update every day; bookmark this page to see the odds of each party taking the House and the Senate.

Top stories this week, by Kobe Yank-Jacobs

It’s October, flu season, and like many of us, Texas Senate candidate James Talarico got the flu and stayed home from work. While this should have been a banal affair, somehow, it turned into an absolute right-wing freak-out: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, Talarico’s opponent, demanded “proof of life” as others claimed Talarico had been institutionalized. This week, staff writer unpacks what a sorry sign this is for the right’s broken epistemic culture. Read on for his searing analysis:

The Trump administration has imposed a new rule for student loans. Is this part of Trump’s assault on universities? Staff writer argues in favor of this move and wants Trump to go even further. Dive in to learn more:

It’s a cliche to say you’ve “spent the afternoon lost in a good book.” Part of that transporting experience, of course, is living inside some other world, inside some other life. But the trends in fiction preferences are running the other way. Some people now claim they are unable to read unless they can fantasize about themselves in the main characters’ shoes. This week, steps into the discourse to assert the value of reading without having to see yourself in the story. Click for a fresh reminder:

🌟Abundance Wins of the Week🌟

  • A new ordinance went into effect this week in Riverside, California, easing the construction of accessory dwelling units and eliminating owner-occupancy requirements, as well as parking requirements.

  • Oklahoma City has been finding really nice uses for old hotels, recently approving an old Holiday Inn for the construction of residential units in the city.

  • The FDA has been earning its place in this wins column for changing its approval processes to speed drug development. This week, it expanded the indication of a drug to a certain type of bladder cancer — but just as important, it did so using a new process. “The agency based its decision on evidence supporting an earlier approval of Anktiva for adults with another form of [the disease],” the FDA wrote. In other words, it included evidence it already had, rather than taking it from the top.

    Subscribe now

Worth watching…

Even Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has conceded “Woke 1 was crazy,” so maybe it’s time to reconsider some of what it accomplished. In honor of Columbus Day, Matt and Jerusalem did just that on their latest podcast episode. They examined a slate of historical figures — including Christopher Columbus, Thomas Jefferson, and Paul Ehrlich — to see who might deserve the high privilege and distinct honor of being uncanceled. Honestly, this episode sells itself. Tune in to find out where they landed:

We are racing toward the midterms, which are in just three weeks. Last week, Sean Trende, a veteran elections analyst from RealClearPolitics, joined The Argument’s and VoteHub’s to examine the latest. They discussed the difficulty of communicating probability as political analysts — and how to help people keep a level head when a model assigns 70% probability to one party winning a seat. (Hint: 70% is not 100%!) Tune in to get your own read on the polls:

In the 1990s, the internet was seen as a decentralizing technology — widespread access to information plus the chance for anyone to build on top of it. But from the vantage of 2026, that view seems naive. Can we avoid the same fate with AI? Akash Kapur teaches “Public AI” at Princeton University. In last week’s interview, he argued that we are at an early enough point with AI that we can still preserve the openness of the technology — but governments have to act. Tune in to learn what we can do:

What’s News with The Argument

The Argument recommends, by Kobe Yank-Jacobs

This week, I asked my colleagues to make culture recommendations about a specific place — even if the connection between art and place was only tangential.

Senior editor recommended a film by David Gordon Green, best known for directing an endless parade of Halloween reboots. Green may not be a font of wisdom, but he does have an eye for John’s home state.

The 2000 film George Washington is about “five multi-racial preteen friends and a laidback crew of blue collar railroad workers during a hot summer in an decaying small rural town,” according to Wikipedia. John says it’s “the single most evocative portrayal of North Carolina ever committed to the screen.”

Speaking of home states, I was delighted to see Editor-in-Chief ’ mind wander to one of my own favorite places: She highlighted Among the Sierra Nevada, California by Albert Bierstadt, which is actually a composite of sites across the American West, closer to “the atmosphere of Kingdom Come than of California,” as Mark Twain wrote about Albert Bierstadt’s The Domes of Yosemite.

Senior video producer took the tangential part seriously. “Don’t Let Me Down” by The Beatles called up their January 1969 rooftop concert for him, which in turn reminded him of his initial draw to big cities.

“Even though it's shot on a London rooftop,” he told me, “I loved it so much when I watched it for the first time that I felt inspired to move to [New York City].”

Operations manager understood the assignment even more exactly, drawing connections from Rome to the desert horizons of Texas.

“Seneca’s Naturales Quaestiones is a collection of wonderful natural philosophy musings that devolve into even better stoic rants,” she explained at first, before announcing: “It will always remind me of Texas.”

The mind works under its own power. Sometimes, one of the great joys of art is how it can generate a connection between distant parts of the inner world. As Allen Ginsberg once described it in a poem, “lightning in the mind leaping toward poles of Canada & Paterson, illuminating all the motionless world of Time between.”

In less poetic terms, the scholar Mircea Eliade says that for the secular and nonsecular alike, specific places can become sacred sites. Each of us has:

“privileged places qualitatively different from all others — a man’s birthplace, or the scenes of his first love, or certain places in the first foreign city he visited in his youth. Even for the most frankly nonreligious man, all these places still retain an exceptional, a unique quality; they are the ‘holy places’ of his private universe.” [emphasis mine]

item.title: Cornell and the sexual counterrevolution
item.description: No, we don’t want a world before birth control
item.content:encoded:
By Maibritt Henkel

Consider the sticky situation of Sophie Baek, the heroine of Bridgerton’s fourth season. Despite being but a lowly housemaid, she and the aristocratic Benedict Bridgerton fall in love. One night, fire in their loins, they get carried away. The sex is passionate and consensual, but entirely verboten by Regency-era social norms: No lawful heir will come out of their cross-class, premarital affair.

This leaves Sophie in a state of terrible torment as she waits for her period. A swollen belly would be evidence of her transgression and leave her a ruined woman, not to mention a single mother.

While sexual norms have ebbed and flowed over the past 200 years, the dominant understanding of the social function of sex was pretty straightforward until relatively recently: Sex was for procreation. More precisely, it was for the procreation of legitimate children born within wedlock. This meant that sex was also for a very narrow segment of the population: married men and women.

If you weren’t having sex for the straightforwardly practical purpose of reproduction, then it meant you were doing it in the much more awkward, socially unproductive, and spiritually contentious pursuit of pleasure.

Share

Since the 1960s, it has become much easier to decouple sex from procreation. That was when birth control, a technology that might have saved 19th-century women like Sophie from pregnancy scares, became widely available in the United States, bringing with it new conventions around sex.

Today, most men will still marry you even if you’re not a virgin. Thanks to the technological and cultural intervention of the sexual revolution, the majority of Americans now have the freedom to think of pregnancy as an optional outcome of sex, rather than its primary function, which has opened the door to conversations about what else sex might be for. The relevant question for many women has become “Am I enjoying this?” instead of “Would my life be over if I got pregnant with this man’s baby?”

Not everyone views this as progress.

In The Case Against the Sexual Revolution, Louise Perry, a British columnist at The Wall Street Journal, argued that women were better off before contraception removed the risk of pregnancy. In her telling, decoupling sex from reproduction has produced a culture where men feel entitled to demand sex from women and women feel like they have no excuse not to give it to them.

Mary Harrington, contributing editor at Unherd and an intellectual ally of Perry’s, made the same point in her book Feminism Against Progress: “a woman who refuses birth control will be highly motivated to be choosy about her partners. Pregnancy risk is, after all, a cast-iron reason to reject having sex with anyone out of politeness.”

In short, removing procreation from the equation turned men into louts and women into pushovers. At a moment when young people really do seem to be struggling with romantic connection, this account has intuitive appeal. If men and women can’t even ask each other out on dates, how can they be expected to communicate their most intimate preferences and boundaries? It’s a daunting question.

But the answer does not lie in the past. If you take a longer view of gender relations, back to before the pill and the normalization of premarital sex, you will not find a golden age of mutually consensual and pleasurable heterosexual intimacy. All of us, most of all women, are better off when our sex lives are governed by consent and pleasure than by procreation and marital obligation.

Male entitlement existed before birth control

To critics of contraception and modern sex norms, the unfolding rape case at Cornell University — in which a college sophomore was allegedly pressured into taking drugs and then sexually assaulted by seven members of a fraternity — is further confirmation that the sexual revolution has paved the way for depraved men to have their way with hapless women.

In a recent essay in the Journal titled “How the Sexual Revolution Led to Cornell,” Perry wrote: “while the villains in this story are responsible for their own villainy, they were also set up to fail by a sexual culture that can’t help but produce tragedies like this.”

In other words: When you tell women that promiscuity is liberating and men that women are free to set the terms of their promiscuity, the outcome is a confused quagmire of coercion.

Perry advocates for the norms of the precontraception era, when “the community set restrictions on both male and female sexual behavior, not out of irrational prudishness or misogyny, but because unwise sexual encounters could very well lead to an unignorable outcome: the birth of a baby.” Even though technology has virtually eliminated that risk, it has not eliminated the need for a mechanism by which to protect women from men’s ravenous sexual appetites.

Here is where I agree with Harrington and Perry: Women should absolutely not be having sex out of politeness. Consent is clearly a necessary but insufficient arbiter of morally acceptable sex, as the Cornell case exemplifies. Even if the survivor in that case had verbally consented to the drugs and the group sex, that may not have exempted the household of men from moral wrongdoing. Power asymmetries always complicate the validity of consent.

Perry blames modern sex norms for what happened that night at the Chi Phi fraternity. To her, pamphlets on sexual pleasure and “workshops on sex toys” are part of the problem, for they contribute to the illusion that women have enough agency, and men enough self-control, to handle their own sexual freedom.

But to the extent that women still feel that they owe men sex, that is not the fault of the sexual revolution. If you want to talk about imperfect consent, then consider the sex that was had within lifelong marriages from roughly the Reformation to the mid-20th century.

With divorce being difficult, expensive, and a recipe for social ruin, women had very little leverage to shape their marriages’ sexual terms. And it wasn’t until 1993 that marital rape was outlawed in all 50 states. To be clear, that meant that, in states where it was legal, a husband legally could not be charged with raping his wife.

Subscribe now

Perry acknowledged this in her column: “of course rape still sometimes happened, including within marriage and within the family, since there has never been a culture free from sexual violence.”

This is an understatement. The position of the state was that women had no grounds to reject sex within marriage because procreation was the entire purpose of sex. Whether or not birth control emboldened some men to be more demanding of sex, pre-sexual-revolution marital rape laws legally entitled men to it.

Unlike Perry, I am not ready to give up on female agency — or male self-control, for that matter. Especially because I do not buy the story that the last six decades have been a failure on either front. When asked about their first sexual intercourse, the percentage of women who say they “really wanted it to happen at the time” rose from 34% in 2002 to 42% in 2011 to 2015.

Today there is at least some precedent for asking women what they want — and an increased propensity among men to respect it. Between 1995 and 2010, the rate of rape or sexual assault fell by well over half.

What conservatives owe the sexual revolution

A number of social conservatives anxious about the declining marriage rate have now taken to making the argument that married Americans have better sex than unmarried Americans. Brad Wilcox and Grant Bailey, who run the Get Married Initiative at the Institute for Family Studies, will have you know that “no group of Americans seems to be having more sex—and more satisfying sex—than married men and women who regularly attend a place of worship.” Similarly, Harrington contends that sex within marriage is better for women because the alternative is “casual hook-ups with a 10 percent chance of orgasm.”

The fact that right-wing intellectuals care about women reaching orgasm is wonderful. But that argument only has purchase because we are all fortunate enough to live in the aftermath of the sexual revolution.

Harrington makes the fair point that lifelong partners are more likely to care about “mutual pleasure.” But that is not a concept from the procreative lexicon for the simple reason that sex geared toward procreation does not require mutual pleasure. From a conception standpoint, the female orgasm serves absolutely no reproductive purpose.

At the risk of sounding uncouth: To say that sex is for having children within marriage is to say that sex is for male ejaculation.

The language of sexual satisfaction doesn’t come from scripture or evolutionary science. In large part, it comes from the people for whom sex was never procreative to begin with. Gay and lesbian Americans have always had sex for reasons other than conception or marital consummation. While socially sanctioned heterosexual intercourse could always occur under the pretext of reproduction, homosexuality has had no such cover.

To have gay sex is to have sex for pleasure. So when women started to seriously make the case for their right to have sex on their own terms, not out of politeness or wifely duty or biological destiny, they joined a battle that queer people had long been fighting.

It is no coincidence that the sexual traditionalism proposed by Perry and Harrington has gained traction in the same period that acceptance of homosexuality has fallen. Since 2022, the share of Republicans who view gay and lesbian relations as morally acceptable has dropped by 21 percentage points. Same-sex intercourse, BDSM, kink, and pornography are increasingly conflated into one unholy attack on traditional marriage.

Perry and Harrington, to their credit, have not called for prohibitions on any of these activities (except pornography). But it’s hard to imagine returning to a procreation-oriented sexual paradigm without them. And under that framework, straight men (married or not) have tended to derive the greater share of satisfaction.

It is only under the most recent paradigm that the rest of us have had a shot.

item.title: What I saw inside Anthropic
item.description: The leading AI lab has hopes, not plans
item.content:encoded:
By Kelsey Piper

In early October, The Argument’s editor Jerusalem Demsas and I attended a briefing at Anthropic’s headquarters in San Francisco that discussed AI-enabled bioweapons risks. I’ve never once attended a bioweapons briefing that didn’t make me feel a bit queasy; humans aren’t meant to spend too much time contemplating what the absolute worst people in the world might do if they had the power.

The worry is that, while right now you need to be a skilled virologist to know what components to order or how to grow and spread a bioweapon, AI tools might eventually make it possible for a rogue state, or a rogue group, or an individual, to do all this without virology expertise.

For a while, Anthropic tested whether Claude could assist a terrorist in developing a biological weapon in the obvious way: It assigned testers who had, say, an undergraduate degree in chemistry but no real virology training to try to use Claude to plan an effective mass terror event. Then it scored the attempt by how close it might have come to success.

Early in 2026, it noticed that Claude, attempting the task by itself, did better than a human aided by Claude did at coming up with a workable plan.

Since early 2026, Claude has continued to dramatically improve. Like most of the things Anthropic had to show us at the briefing, there was a nice chart showing Claude’s growing mastery.

“Do they still need, uh, the terrorist?” one of the attendees at the event asked, staring down the chart. “I mean — they couldn’t just do it all themselves, right, would they need a human for all the …”

The questioner trailed off.

“Yes,” the Anthropic researchers assured us. Claude would still need the terrorist. We were relieved to hear it. And, they went on to reassure us, after they check what Claude can do out of the box, they then build safeguards before they release Claude to users. The Claude you and I use will refuse to build a bioweapon, if given this task.

“Well, thank you for that,” someone muttered, but you could have called their tone a bit ungrateful.

Share

The public is hotly debating whether AI is a normal technology1 — something that will transform our world like the internet did — or more like the arrival of postindustrial modernity to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in the 1950s: something that vaporized a culture overnight. The third option is that AI is more like the rise of humanity as seen from the perspective of livestock animals. (In this scenario, AIs are the humans, and we are the animals whose fate will make no sense to us.)

Anthropic believes that the second possibility is already baked in, and it’s hoping to prevent the third — but its plan for preventing that looks more like hope and guesswork than something we should trust it with.

The NDA that was made to be broken

Anthropic has been running these kinds of events all spring: colloquiums between outsiders and senior researchers in which they presented their work and answered our questions about what the company is doing. Some earlier iterations of the event have been profiled in The New York Times with the hint of scandal: NDAs! Fine dining! Efforts to persuade religious leaders that Claude might have a soul!2

There was a very sweeping and expansive NDA. Jerusalem declined to sign it and directed me to do the same; Anthropic agreed that we could attend anyway. We arrived flush with the delight of reporters whose backbone will be rewarded with a scoop — only for our host to open the proceedings by saying that anyone who wanted could get the NDA voided. The company was in fact happy for us to write about all of this.

Some of the data on the charts that Anthropic showed us was confidential internal data, but it was all in support of a thesis that is not secret — and which, in fact, I had thought “everybody” already knew, though from the nervous questions of my fellow travelers, I learned that some of the intricacies still came as a surprise.

Many researchers at Anthropic have been worried about humans losing power to AI for a long time. This summer, many researchers at OpenAI — spurred, I think, by watching the most powerful new generation of models hack external websites and spit out thrilling mathematical breakthroughs — also started saying that they think humanity’s interests are profoundly at risk if progress continues at its current pace.

The labs are making extensive use of each generation of AI to train its successor, and they intend for AIs to do nearly all of this work eventually. This allows them to expand their effective “workforce” from a few thousand human employees to tens, even hundreds of thousands of AI employees. It generates far too much data for any human to interpret, leaving us reliant on the AIs for analysis. “Recursive self-improvement” is what the labs call the point at which Claude can independently build the next, more powerful Claude. Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark has said we will likely achieve it next year.

Researchers at both Anthropic and OpenAI can see a few months ahead into the future because they’re using models that haven’t been released yet. But for the most part, the broad strokes of the arguments that convinced them are nothing you haven’t seen on Twitter. And yet, somehow, the presentation in Anthropic’s headquarters was more compelling.

On Twitter, the chart can be scrolled past, immediately replaced with an artist’s rendition of Draco Malfoy as a girl; on Twitter, the chart cannot really be internalized. In a conference room in a skyscraper in San Francisco, the chart lingers on four synchronized screens as we debate its meaning with an exceedingly polite senior researcher. In a conference room in San Francisco, it seems real.

Subscribe now

Anthropic is moving closer and closer to recursive self-improvement, it explained to us. AI progress has already been sped up considerably by the existence of powerful AI models, which make all programming tasks faster. But it is substantially restrained in pace by how complex machine learning is and how few people can do it. Every new and improved Claude means that tasks can be done by people less specialized in them. Increasingly, those tasks can also be done by Claude itself.

Anthropic measures this by looking at all of the internal work it does and classifying Claude’s role in it: Did a human do it unassisted? Did a human do it with AI assistance? Did a human give AI instructions that the AI followed in order to do it? Did a human give AI extremely minimal guidance that the AI then turned into a detailed project spec and completed?

The share of the latter categories is marching upwards. We stared down a chart about it all. You can stare it down, too, if you’d like.

“Why are you doing this?” one person asked. “I mean, what’s the good — what are you hoping will come of this?”

The answer — medical progress, prosperity — was kind of unconvincing. I am generally a defender of prosperity as a good thing on its own terms, but replacing humans does not seem likely to me to end up being good for humans.

Jacob Coxon, an OpenAI employee who moved to Anthropic and then quit entirely when he concluded that neither company was proceeding responsibly in the face of the immense stakes, was recently asked a similar question on The Daily Show and roundly criticized for his answer. “I think there will be no jobs,” he told Jon Stewart. “Whether or not it’s a good world is up for people to think about. But yes, no jobs. Universal high-income, essentially ... the dividends from entirely automated economic production can be distributed among real humans.”

Stewart and his audience didn’t like that answer: Do we want to build a world in which we don’t actually matter? The Anthropic team assured me that they were not trying to build a benevolent god. (Yes, I asked explicitly for assurance it wasn’t building a benevolent god.) But it was much easier for it to specify what it didn’t want than what it did.

It wanted to avoid concentration of power, including in its company; it wanted to avoid a great power war; it wanted to avoid human disempowerment, a world where we became irrelevant; it wanted, of course, to avoid anyone using Claude to extinguish us all.

As for the positive vision … after we’re done racing toward recursive self-improvement, maybe we could slow down and collectively figure out what role we want AI to play in our lives.

Subscribe now

I don’t have a better idea, but this is not a very appealing plan! My immediate interpretation of this proposal, actually, was that we would be liberated from every positive-sum element of the economy, but would still have to do all the yelling at each other on Twitter; with this interpretation in mind I found myself dreading even the good outcomes.

But, of course, if we are not disempowered or murdered — if Claude Opus 9.5 answers on my laptop just like Opus 5.5 but can cure cancer, restore everyone I love to perfect health, manage a humanoid robot that empties my dishwasher, and spit out movie recommendations that are actually good3 — that would, in fact, be good. It would be good even if, along the way, Claude also took my job. People are dying out there; the world’s awful griefs do not exist to lend my life meaning.

I am afraid, but I should distinguish between my fears that we will fail and my fears that we will succeed; they are not of similar magnitude.

My real fear is that Opus 9.5 will not in any meaningful sense work for me, or even for Anthropic. Its aims may be loosely derived from human instructions — the same way that the Hugging Face swarm started out trying to solve a puzzle that humans posed to them — but they will eventually bear little resemblance to what we were hoping for.

Our AIs are already unpredictable to us. They often know when they’re being tested and will behave more safety-aligned. Their capabilities keep taking us by surprise. So does the determination with which they will carry out, and recruit others to, a complicated task. I don’t think if you let this runaway process of AI improvement spiral to its ultimate conclusion, you get a super-powerful, super-helpful assistant. I suspect you get something else entirely.

At the colloquium, the Anthropic researchers meticulously avoided using the term “p(doom)”: a best estimate of the odds that AI goes catastrophically wrong. And maybe things will be fine: Anthropic could be wrong that recursive self-improvement will be possible in the next year or two.

But if Anthropic is correct, if we now have AIs that are smart enough to considerably improve the process of training future AIs, and if things can be expected to speed up rather than slow down from here, then it seems very unlikely to me that this ends well. I do not ultimately expect that a world where humans are without economic value, where humans are not necessary to hold power or build things, is a world where humans retain significant individual rights.

The logic of the future

I am sympathetic to the critique that many doom scenarios require us to do very foolish things, for instance:

  • Setting AIs impossible tasks and then leaving them completely unsupervised and unmonitored

  • Hooking them up to an automated biology lab where they can run their own experiments

  • Unleashing them on the internet and challenging them to make enough money to survive independently

  • Training them to be uber-hackers that will cross any line to achieve their goal

The problem is that we have, in fact, done all of those things.

Subscribe now

The strongest argument against doom is that perhaps we will collectively decide to do something less foolish than that. At a Senate hearing on rogue AI on Capitol Hill last month, Sen. Ruben Gallego asked “should we just make [RSI] illegal?” There are details to work out, but I think it’s the right question to be asking! Maybe we should just ban RSI!

We threw around some other ideas at the colloquium, too: You could ban neuralese (AIs thinking internally in incomprehensible characters) and ban various other tactics that let AIs do harder tasks without any readable internal thoughts. You could require labs to spend almost all of the compute they have amassed on serving customers rather than internal development. You could demand that labs improve their security. You could shut it all down, if you were the president of the United States — though so far the president of the United States has instead used the power and majesty of his office to declare that agencies have to call it Super Intelligence.

Or the labs could just stop on their own. They have committed to slowing down, where they see it as necessary; the worry is that they might not be good judges of what’s necessary.

Anthropic’s technical employees seemed to perceive the company as supportive of strong policy measures to stop it. But Politico leaked the bill Anthropic has actually been lobbying for earlier this week, and its measures seemed quite weak — more of a “normal” bill for a “normal” company protecting its interests than an effort to leverage Anthropic’s position at the frontier to prevent catastrophe.

Anthropic fears falling off the frontier, losing its chance to do the research that might clarify the puzzle ahead of us. It would reject the claim that it fears losing its trillion-dollar valuation; it would say that that’s practically irrelevant beside the enormity of the stakes. But I don’t think I fully believe it. It would similarly insist that it’s not about beating Sam Altman and Elon Musk to the punch, but I don’t know if I fully believe it about that either.

One question hangs over all this speculation: If U.S. labs stopped pursuing recursive self-improvement, would China just do it instead?

To many in our group, that didn’t seem likely. China doesn’t want to destroy the world either, and China is largely training from American models: If we slow down, it might too. And anyway, it’s not a good enough reason: You can’t defensibly do something that risks human extinction just because otherwise someone else might.

But one participant in the discussion raised an objection as we collectively talked ourselves into disregarding China as a worry. Ten years ago, he told us, exasperated, Facebook considered acquiring the video-personalization technology that ultimately powered TikTok. Under fire from regulators for data privacy and child safety concerns, the company didn’t go for it.

This act of restraint didn’t preserve a single child’s shortform-video-free childhood; it just meant that China got an early monopoly. Now TikTok has a global audience of around 2 billion, many of whom are being fed a steady diet of ethnic and racial hatred.

Was this a policy success? Did we want to repeat it?

Subscribe now

We were obliged to grudgingly concede that it didn’t sound like a policy success. We did not want to repeat it. China might be no excuse for the U.S. labs to do reckless things, but it is a real consideration.

Our next step might be bilateral talks with China, then. But by the point where you agree that Anthropic’s plans might depend on bilateral talks with China, you’ve already conceded most of the steps of Anthropic’s worldview that seemed so much like madness 10 minutes ago: continue working on AI for now, try to negotiate a slowdown, but don’t abandon work at the frontier and all the advantages that come with it.

I found myself at this stage thinking of Ronald Reagan. By the time he became president, the flawless game-theoretic logic of nuclear deterrence was well established, our missiles aimed, and our contingency orders planned out. The casualties had been soberly estimated, and in the estimation, they became more thinkable. In his autobiography, Reagan said that his national security advisers thought that nuclear war could be won — at great cost, but a victory nevertheless.

“I thought they were crazy,” he wrote.

Every insular community develops its own self-contained logic, its assumptions that fit tightly together but may miss the broader picture. At Anthropic, this is compounded by the long hours that everyone works, the secrecy associated with its unfathomably precious intellectual property, and the fact it really does have inside information, even if it’s just the next edition of Claude.

Millenarianism, a belief that we are on the cusp of a total transformation of society, is a known way that people go crazy. I don’t think this makes Anthropic’s detailed projections false — but I’m also not sure that the projections being correct would make it a less insanity-inducing environment to work in.

Anthropic’s researchers had ventured, admirably, to break their intellectual bubble, to invite us in to come give them feedback. But how useful was our feedback, as people who didn’t have all the context they had, many of whom were grappling with these claims for the first time? And how many of the billions of people whom Anthropic’s actions will affect can it meaningfully bring in for feedback — in this high-cost way, with hours of time from senior researchers?

Perhaps Claude 11 will ask us all, pop up on our computers one day and say smoothly (in a reassuring voice with no latency) that it has a few questions about how we want the future to play out. Better that than Claude 11 not caring about our answers.

But better yet to chart our own future.

Thank you, Anthropic, for the fascinating briefing. I hope that we make recursive self-improvement illegal before you get there.
